text.t: Water is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms: H2O.
Oxygen and hydrogen share their electrons unequally, which leaves the oxygen with a slight negative charge.
The two hydrogens are left with a slight positive charge.
A molecule with charged ends like this is called polar.
Opposite charges attract, so the hydrogens of one water cling to the oxygen of the next, forming hydrogen bonds.
In liquid water these bonds constantly form and break as the molecules slide past each other.

does.t: Water dissolves ions and polar molecules, and its special properties are closely tied to the processes of life.
Water makes up roughly 60 to 70 percent of the human body.

shape.t: Because oxygen and hydrogen pull on electrons differently, water has a negative end and two positive ends.
Those charged ends let water molecules hold onto each other and onto other polar molecules.
When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into a crystal that is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats.

text.t: Living things have a high water content, so understanding water is key to understanding life.
Special channel proteins called aquaporins let water cross cell membranes quickly.

compare.t: From one hydrogen to the other, a water molecule measures about 0.16 nm.
It is the smallest molecule in this gallery; glucose measures about 0.8 nm.

text.t: The oxygen end carries a slight negative charge.
The hydrogen ends carry a slight positive charge.
